Practice Problem 2: Cost Accounting at Youkea
Youkea is an upcoming Scandinavian office furniture retailer that is just establishing itself in the New England area. Youkea has specialized in office chairs. While they have three stores, their Boston branch is serving only business customers, and act as a combined warehouse and store for the Boston Area business customers.

To assess the profitability of different business customers at the Boston branch, Youkea has used a simple mark-up to allocate overhead costs to customers based on volume (number of chairs). This means that larger customers have been allocated a larger share of overhead costs. A manager at Youkea is now suspecting this to be misleading, since customers consume very different amounts of the resources that generate overhead costs.

One difference is in order handling. There are currently two ways for customers to order chairs from Youkea: through Youkea's webpage or over the phone. Orders that come in over the phone need to be entered manually into the system, line by line. As a result, the cost of handling a phone order depends on the number of order lines. Orders that come in through the webpage can be easily transferred into the system and only incurs a one-per-order order entry cost. Last year, Youkea processed 700 orders, for a combined total of 4,800 chairs. 20% of the orders were made over the phone, for a total of 800 order lines. The order entry costs associated with these phone orders represented 85% of total order entry costs.

Customers also differ in how the chairs are delivered to them. A customer may use the default option of common carrier delivery. For such deliveries, Youkea pays the carrier based on the number of chairs. For instance, delivering two chairs to a customer costs Youkea twice as much as delivering one chair. However, a customer may instead choose to receive express delivery using Youkea's own distribution truck, which is operated by Youkea personnel. The cost of these deliveries depends only on the number of shipments. That is, delivering one chair is just as costly to Youkea as delivering two chairs to the same customer. Last year, 100 such express deliveries were made by Youkea's own truck, delivering a total of 800 chairs.

All chairs that are delivered to customers from the Boston branch have arrived from a distribution center. Costs in the warehouse area of the branch tend to depend on the throughput.

Based on this, the manager believes that an activity based approach to assessing the cost of the customers at the Boston branch may be in place.

supply_chain_design.label: Exercise 01
supply_chain_design.text: Students engaged briefly with supplier selection and total cost calculation, with the tutor using effective Socratic questioning to guide students through the formula structure while preserving their opportunity to complete the analysis independently. The interaction demonstrates that students grasped the mechanics of total cost comparison once the framework was clarified, requiring only confirmation and redirection rather than extended explanation of the underlying concepts.

supply_chain_design.label: Practice 7
supply_chain_design.text: Students engaged with a wide range of topics across supplier selection, cost analysis, optimization modeling, and procurement strategy. Most conversations were brief, with many consisting of single exchanges that limited the depth of interaction; however, tutors generally employed Socratic questioning effectively in these short interactions, guiding students to compute costs, set up decision variables, and derive formulas rather than providing direct answers. Common areas of difficulty included understanding total cost of ownership and its component parts, formulating constraints and decision variables for optimization problems (particularly in multi-lane procurement scenarios), and distinguishing between providing guidance and revealing submission-ready answers. A few conversations showed tutors crossing into direct problem-solving—providing complete constraint formulas, fully structured methodologies, or near-final numerical answers before students had derived them—which undermined the guided discovery approach. Several conversations also lacked initial diagnostic questioning or were structured with multiple embedded questions that may have overwhelmed students rather than inviting focused engagement. A small number of conversations had no tutor response at all or consisted only of off-topic clarification requests, limiting substantive learning on the assignment content.

supply_chain_design.label: Practice 8
supply_chain_design.text: Students engaged with a broad range of activity-based costing and cost allocation topics, with most conversations centering on cost-to-serve analysis, driver rate calculations, and the mechanics of ABC template structure. The most common areas of difficulty were correctly identifying and assigning cost drivers, distinguishing between per-unit and per-batch data when computing driver rates, and understanding how traditional overhead allocation differs from activity-based approaches. Several students struggled with depreciation calculations (particularly depreciation period and salvage value treatment) and with mapping specific cost line items to the correct activity pools. Most tutoring interactions were brief but pedagogically sound, with tutors consistently using Socratic questioning to guide students through reasoning rather than providing direct answers; however, a few conversations showed instances where tutors either pre-emptively laid out full solution roadmaps or performed key computational steps for students before they had attempted them independently. Overall, students received appropriately scaffolded support, though some would have benefited from more concise, focused prompts rather than multi-part questions delivered simultaneously.

supply_chain_design.label: Practice 9
supply_chain_design.text: Students engaged with the core valuation concepts in this practice, focusing on perpetuity formulas, NPV calculations, and the mechanics of free cash flow projections—particularly how working capital components like accounts receivable, inventory, and accounts payable affect timing and cash flow. The conversations were brief but pedagogically sound, with tutors consistently using Socratic questioning to guide students toward the formulas and logic rather than providing direct answers. The main area where students needed support was understanding how to properly discount cash flows over time and how working capital timing interacts with the valuation model, suggesting these remain conceptually challenging elements that benefit from guided discovery rather than immediate solutions.
